Ancient Greek poet traditionally credited as the author of the [[Iliad|*Iliad*]] and the [[Odyssey|*Odyssey*]], two epic poems foundational to [[Ancient Greek literature]]. The *Iliad* centers on a quarrel between King Agamemnon and the warrior Achilles during the last year of the [[Trojan War]]. The *Odyssey* chronicles the ten-year journey of Odysseus, king of Ithaca, back home after the fall of [[Troy]]. Most researchers believe they were originally transmitted orally, and they are thought to have been composed around the late eighth or early seventh century BC.

Homer's identity and existence, the "Homeric Question," remain debated, and scholars generally regard the ancient conception of a single author as a fictional narrative. Many accounts of his life circulated in antiquity, the most widespread portraying him as a blind bard from Ionia, a region on the western coast of Anatolia, or from the islands of Chios and Samos. Other traditions named Smyrna, Argos, and Athens as his birthplace. Modern scholars consider these accounts apocryphal or "legendary." In antiquity many other works were attributed to him, including the Homeric Hymns, but these claims are not considered authentic today.

The poems shaped Greek culture and education, fostering ideals of heroism, glory, and honor. [[Plato]] described Homer as the one who "has educated Greece." In Dante's *Divine Comedy*, [[Virgil]] calls him "Poet sovereign," and [[Alexander Pope]] acknowledged in the preface to his translation of the *Iliad* that Homer has always been considered the "greatest of poets." The epics have inspired many works of literature, music, art, and film.

Act by which one person causes the death of another. Homicide requires only a volitional act, or an omission, that causes death, so it may result from accidental, reckless, or negligent acts even without intent to cause harm. Its overlapping legal categories include [[Murder|murder]], manslaughter, justifiable homicide, [[Assassination|assassination]], killing in [[War|war]] (lawful or as a war crime), [[Euthanasia|euthanasia]], and [[Capital punishment|capital punishment]].

Criminal homicide is divided into murder and manslaughter according to the perpetrator's state of mind and intent. Murder is the most serious charge. First-degree murder is the premeditated, unlawful, intentional killing of another person; second-degree murder is intentional and unlawful but without premeditation. In the United States, under the felony murder rule, a person committing a felony may be guilty of murder if someone dies as a result, regardless of intent. Manslaughter is voluntary, an intentional but unpremeditated killing in heat of passion, or involuntary, an unintentional killing through recklessness or negligence. The distinction between murder and manslaughter is sometimes said to have first been made by the Athenian lawmaker [[Draco (legislator)|Draco]] in the 7th century BC.

Not all homicides are prosecutable. Common defenses and excuses include self-defense, [[Mental disorder|mental incapacity]], the defense of infancy, and justifiable homicide, such as a lawful killing in battle.

A report by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime in July 2019 documented nearly 464,000 homicide deaths worldwide in 2017, against 89,000 killed in armed conflicts. Another estimate gives approximately 458,000 in 2021, with the [[Americas]] showing the highest rates.

Special administrative region of China (pop., mid-2025: c. 7.53 million), on the southern coast just south of [[Shenzhen]]. It comprises Hong Kong Island, the Kowloon Peninsula, the New Territories, and over 260 outlying islands, with an area of 1,114 sq km, making it the fourth-most densely populated region in the world.

The area was first incorporated into China under the [[Qin dynasty]] in 214 BC. After the Qing dynasty lost the [[First Opium War]], it ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain in 1841–1842, and the colony expanded to Kowloon in 1860 and, through a 99-year lease of the New Territories, in 1898. Japan occupied the territory from 1941 to 1945 during [[World War II]]. Sovereignty passed from the United Kingdom to China in 1997 under the Sino-British Joint Declaration. Under "one country, two systems," Hong Kong keeps separate governing and economic systems, with autonomy in all affairs except foreign affairs and defense pledged until 2047.

Originally farming and fishing villages, Hong Kong is one of the world's most significant financial centres, ranked third globally behind [[New York City]] and [[London]]. The Hong Kong dollar is the ninth-most traded currency, and the city has more skyscrapers than any other. It has a [[Human Development Index]] of 0.955, ranking eighth in the world, the highest life expectancy in the world, though severe income inequality persists.

Political change followed the 2019–2020 protests and the 2020 National Security Law, which the National People's Congress enacted in place of local legislation and which criminalizes secession, subversion, terrorism, and foreign collusion. Critics argue that it has diminished civil liberties and judicial independence, while Chinese and Hong Kong officials describe it as restoring stability.

Class of signaling molecules in multicellular organisms, sent to distant organs or tissues to regulate physiology and behavior. The term derives from Ancient Greek *hormôn*, "setting in motion." Because the definition is broad, many kinds of molecules qualify, including eicosanoids, [[Steroid|steroids]], amino acid derivatives such as epinephrine and auxin, proteins and peptides such as [[Insulin|insulin]], and gases such as [[Ethylene|ethylene]] and [[Nitric oxide|nitric oxide]].

In [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]], hormones, produced by glands of the [[Endocrine system]], regulate processes including digestion, metabolism, respiration, sensory perception, sleep, excretion, lactation, stress, growth, reproduction, and mood. In [[Plant|plants]], they modulate almost all aspects of development, from germination to senescence. Plants lack specialized hormone-secreting organs.

A hormone acts by binding to specific receptor proteins in a target cell, activating a signal transduction pathway that typically triggers gene transcription and increased expression of target proteins. Water-soluble hormones, such as peptides and amines, generally act on the cell surface through second messengers. Lipid-soluble hormones, such as steroids, generally pass through the plasma membrane to act within the nucleus.

In vertebrates, endocrine glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream, whereas the exocrine system uses ducts. Secretion is often subject to negative feedback: high blood sugar promotes insulin synthesis, and insulin then lowers glucose levels, leading to reduced insulin levels. Imbalances can cause disorders such as [[Diabetes|diabetes]] and hypothyroidism. In 1849 the German physiologist Arnold Adolph Berthold observed that castrated roosters had reduced secondary sexual organs and no sexual or aggressive behavior.

Domesticated, one-toed, hoofed [[Mammal|mammal]] (*Equus ferus caballus*) of the family [[Equidae]]. The horse evolved over the past 45 to 55 million years from a small multi-toed creature, *Eohippus*, originally in North America. Humans began [[Domestication|domesticating]] horses around 4000 BC in [[Central Asia]], primarily associated with the Botai culture, and domestication is believed to have been widespread by 3000 BC. Genetic evidence indicates, however, that modern breeds descend not from this lineage but from horses of the lower Volga-Don region, which spread across Eurasia from 2000 BC.

Horses are non-ruminant [[Herbivore|herbivores]] adapted to run, and can sleep both standing and lying down. Mares carry their young for approximately 11 months. Most domesticated horses begin training under a [[Saddle|saddle]] or in harness at two to four years, and live on average 25 to 30 years; the oldest verifiable record is a 19th-century horse that lived to 62. Light-riding horses usually stand 14 to 16 hands (142 to 163 cm; one hand is 101.6 mm) at the withers and weigh 380 to 550 kg.

More than 300 breeds exist. They are broadly classed by temperament as spirited "hot-blooded" horses known for speed and endurance, "cold-blooded" draft horses and some ponies suited to heavy work, and "warm-bloods" produced by crossing the two. A young horse is a foal, a female four or older a mare, an uncastrated male four or older a stallion, and a castrated male a gelding.

Horses take part in sport, recreation, police work, agriculture, and therapy, and were historically used in warfare. Products derived from them include meat, milk, hide, hair, bone, and pharmaceuticals extracted from the urine of pregnant mares.

[[Health care]] institution providing patient treatment with specialized medical science, staff, and equipment. Hospitals are usually distinguished from smaller clinics by their ability to admit and care for inpatients overnight or longer, while outpatients are treated and leave. The best-known type is the general, or acute-care, hospital, which typically has an [[Emergency department]] for urgent health problems. Specialized hospitals include trauma centers, rehabilitation hospitals, children's and geriatric hospitals, and [[Psychiatric hospital|psychiatric hospitals]]. A teaching hospital combines patient care with training of health science students and of medical graduates completing postgraduate residencies.

Hospitals have departments such as surgery and urgent care, specialist units such as cardiology, and support units including a pharmacy, [[Pathology|pathology]], and [[Radiology|radiology]]. Hospitals are staffed by physicians, surgeons, nurses, and allied health professionals, and are typically funded by public funding, health organizations, insurers, or charities.

The word derives from the [[Latin]] *hospes*, meaning a stranger or guest, and hospitals were originally "places of hospitality," a sense preserved in names such as the Royal Hospital Chelsea, established in 1681 as a retirement and nursing home for veteran soldiers. In the [[Middle Ages]] they served as almshouses for the poor and hostels for pilgrims. Precursors include temple-based healing centers in ancient Mesopotamia, Greece, India, and Sri Lanka, and a comprehensive medical facility established by St. Basil in AD 369. Hospitals were often founded and funded by Christian religious orders or charitable individuals.

Potential and expressed capacity of individuals or groups, mentally, physically, and socially, to respond to internal and external stimuli throughout life. Behavior is driven by environmental and genetic factors and, in part, by thoughts and feelings, which reveal attitudes and values.

The term covers many domains. Social behavior concerns actions directed at others and is shaped by interaction, culture, ethics, politics, and conflict; its acceptability depends on [[Social norm|social norms]] and is regulated by various means of [[Social control|social control]]. Cognitive behavior concerns obtaining and using knowledge, including learning, creativity, and belief. Physiological behavior maintains the body, and economic and ecological behavior concern work and interaction with the environment.

The study of human behavior is interdisciplinary. The social sciences, including [[Psychology|psychology]], [[Sociology|sociology]], and [[Ethology|ethology]], approach it alongside [[Neurology|neurology]] and evolutionary biology, which examine how the nervous system controls behavior and how the human mind evolved. [[Philosophy]] and literature treat the subject outside formal science, with philosophy of mind considering free will and the malleability of behavior. Methods include questionnaires, interviews, and experiments, and [[Twin|twin]] studies are a common way of separating genetic from environmental influences.

The nature versus nurture debate, over whether behavior is predominantly affected by genetic or environmental factors, is a fundamental division in the field. Twin and meta-analytic studies estimate average heritability across traits at 49%, while researchers increasingly emphasize complex interactions among biological, psychological, social, cultural, and environmental factors. The relative weight of deterministic biological causes against volitional or cultural ones remains a subject of controversy.

Physical structure of the human organism, composed of many types of cells that together form tissues, then organs, and then organ systems. The external body consists of a head, neck, torso (including the thorax and abdomen), arms, hands, legs, and feet. The internal body includes organs, teeth, bones, muscles, tendons, ligaments, blood vessels and blood, and lymphatic vessels and lymph. It is studied through [[Anatomy|anatomy]], [[Physiology|physiology]], histology, and embryology by health professionals, physiologists, anatomists, and artists. Many systems interact to maintain homeostasis, keeping substances such as sugar, iron, and oxygen in the blood at safe levels.

The body is composed of elements including hydrogen, oxygen, carbon, calcium, and phosphorus. The adult male body is about 60% water, some 42 litres, of which about 23 litres lies inside cells. At maturity there are roughly 30 trillion [[Cell (biology)|cells]] and 38 trillion bacteria in the body, according to one estimate. Each cell sustains on average tens of thousands of instances of DNA damage per day, which if not repaired correctly may lead to mutations.

There are four main types of [[Tissue (biology)|tissue]]: lining cells (epithelia), connective tissue, nerve tissue, and muscle tissue. [[Organ (biology)|Organs]] are structured collections of cells with a specific function, and most sit within cavities such as the abdomen and pleura. The [[Heart|heart]] lies in the thoracic cavity between the lungs and slightly to the left. It has two atria and two ventricles. [[Coronary artery disease]] is the leading cause of death worldwide, accounting for 16% of all deaths. Eleven major organ systems are commonly distinguished, among them the skeletal, muscular, nervous, endocrine, and digestive systems.

Species of [[Primate|primate]] (*Homo sapiens*, "wise man"), the only extant member of the genus *Homo*, characterized by [[Bipedalism|bipedalism]], minimal body hair, and large, complex brains. It is the most abundant and widespread primate species, with over 8.3 billion individuals occupying almost all regions of Earth.

Humans are highly social, living in structures from families and kinship networks to political states. Their social interactions have established values, norms, and rituals. Curiosity and the desire to understand and influence the environment have motivated art, science, philosophy, religion, mythology, and other fields of knowledge. A large, highly developed prefrontal cortex supports episodic memory, flexible facial expressions, self-awareness, theory of mind, introspection, imagination, and mental time travel. Cumulative preservation and advancement of knowledge across generations is known in anthropology as the ratchet effect.

Humans are omnivorous, have used fire to cook food, and can survive up to eight weeks without food and three or four days without water. They sleep on average seven to nine hours per day. Childbirth carries a high risk of complications and death, and offspring are helpless at birth and typically cared for by both parents. Any two humans are on average over 99% genetically similar, with the most diverse populations in Africa; the genetic difference between males and females is around 1% to 2%. On average, males have greater body strength, and females a higher body fat percentage, longer life span in almost every population, and menopause, after which they are infertile. Gender roles have varied historically.

The species name was coined by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1735. Humans belong to the great apes ([[Hominidae]]); the lineage split from chimpanzees and bonobos around 4–8 million years ago, during which chromosome 2 formed from two others, leaving 23 pairs of chromosomes against 24 in other apes. The genus *Homo* evolved from [[Australopithecus]]. The earliest named species include [[Homo habilis]] and *Homo rudolfensis*, by 2.3 million years ago, and *H. erectus*, which evolved 2 million years ago and was the first to leave Africa. *Homo sapiens* emerged in Africa at least 300,000 years ago and migrated out in at least two waves, gradually replacing or interbreeding with archaic humans. Humans began exhibiting behavioral modernity about 160,000–70,000 years ago, and possibly earlier.

Early humans were hunter-gatherers until [[Agriculture|agriculture]] and animal domestication led to permanent settlement in the [[Fertile Crescent]] and other cradles of civilization. Food surpluses enabled denser populations, governance, and writing. Humans have visited the Moon, and industrialization has contributed significantly to pollution and to the ongoing mass extinction of other forms of life.

Evolutionary process by which *Homo sapiens* arose from earlier primates. Over this history humans gradually developed traits such as [[Bipedalism|bipedalism]], dexterity, and complex language. Modern humans interbred with archaic humans, so their evolution was not linear but weblike.

[[Primate|Primates]] diverged from other mammals about 85 million years ago, in the Late Cretaceous, with the earliest fossils appearing over 55 million years ago in the Paleocene. One of the oldest known primate-like mammals, *Plesiadapis*, came from North America and another, *Archicebus*, from China. Fossils from the Faiyum depression southwest of Cairo record the population that gave rise to all extant primates, including the great apes. Orangutans diverged from the African great apes about 14 million years ago.

Hominins parted from the gorilla lineage between 8 and 9 million years ago. The australopithecines, which include the extinct biped ancestors of humans, separated from the genus *Pan*, containing chimpanzees and bonobos, 4–7 million years ago. Human DNA is 98–99% similar to that of the [[Chimpanzee|chimpanzee]]. The earliest potential hominins, such as *Sahelanthropus* from Chad, date to 7–6 million years ago, and *Ardipithecus ramidus* from [[Ethiopia]], about 4.4 million years ago, combined climbing with upright walking. [[Australopithecus]] flourished from 4 to 2 million years ago; its fully bipedal forms include *A. afarensis*, represented by the skeleton known as [[Lucy (hominid)|Lucy]], discovered in 1974.

The genus *Homo* is evidenced by [[Homo habilis]] over 2 million years ago. *Homo erectus*, from about 1.9 million years ago, had larger brains, used fire, and spread from Africa to Eurasia. *Homo heidelbergensis* gave rise to the [[Neanderthal|Neanderthals]] and to *Homo sapiens*. Anatomically modern humans emerged about 300,000 years ago, and non-African populations carry 1–4% Neanderthal DNA.
